pair01.why: The two are close to identical in order and wording. A's "so merging it does not change behavior until the flag is turned on" and B's "With it off, nothing changes for users" do the same job. Both ask for a Firefox check and set the rename apart. Nothing separates them.

pair02.why: A puts bold headers over one-line bullet lists ("**Testing**", "**Other changes**") and adds the filler "This is a rename only.", which reads like a template. B is a little wordier ("The wait between attempts is capped at 30 seconds") but reads as a person writing. It also asks the reviewers to act: "please check that browser if you can."

pair03.why: B opens with what support should do: "If a customer contacts you about a card being declined... tell them to try the payment again," followed by "not charged." A spends its first two sentences on the incident and reaches the instruction only in its third paragraph. Both carry every needed fact.

A: has not committed to anything with any vendor
B: has not replied to Vendor B's sales rep

pair04.why: B repeats the bullet list in prose: "Vendor B is the cheapest, but it fails Legal's requirement. Vendor A fails Security's." It also states "I haven't replied," which the task never supplied. A is tighter and ends with a useful offer: "Let me know if you want to go through the test projects."

pair05.why: Both are sound. B uses stock setup lines ("The two cheaper options each miss one requirement:", "both hard requirements:") and states C's features twice. A adds the useful cost gap, "$50 a month more than A and $130 more than B," though it repeats the approval question at the end.

A: nothing on the export is waiting on design input

pair06.why: A's "Probably not Friday" clashes with its own "we can ship Friday" if the fix lands. It also asserts "nothing on the export is waiting on design input," which the writer could not know. B gives a consistent yes-if in four sentences: "if the fix slips past Thursday, the export misses this week's deploy."

pair07.why: A has the vague subject "recommendation and approval request", stiff lines ("Two requirements apply.", "Here is how the three vendors compare:") and a "not only on their websites" contrast. B uses the same contrast ("not on their pricing pages"), but its subject carries the ask and the deadline. It also says plainly why the cheaper options are out: "I don't see them as real alternatives."

pair08.why: B is a chat reply dressed as a report: "Short answer:", "Where it stands:", "The risks I see:" with bullets, plus a long closing plan. A gives the same conditional, "Maybe. It ships Friday only if the date fix lands Thursday... before the freeze at 3pm Friday," in three short paragraphs, which suits the channel.

pair09.why: A opens with "The incident is resolved." and gives support its own "What support should do" section. B starts with the incident timeline, uses report-style bold labels ("**Customer impact:**", "**What caused it:**") and puts the retry instruction last.

B: most of the 140 removed lines were the polling code

pair10.why: A puts the flag and its default-off safety in the first two sentences. Its Firefox request names what to check: "check that updates arrive and that the page reconnects." B claims "most of them the polling code," which the task never said, and follows a more standard PR template.

pair11.why: Both are natural chat replies with all three needed facts and the same "I'll post here Thursday" close. A's "Yes, if the last bug fix lands on Thursday" is a cleaner yes-if than B's "Probably, but." A also states the stakes directly: "the export won't make Friday."

pair12.why: A's first three sentences give support everything it needs: it's working, "tell them to try the payment again," and "They were not charged." B opens only with the resolution and puts the instruction behind a bold label. It also adds the reassurance "It should go through," which the facts don't support.
